## The AI "Slop" Aesthetic: Horse Pin Horrors

The ongoing conversation about the uncanny valley of AI-generated advertising reached new peaks this week with the discovery of what has been dubbed the ultimate "Facebook Slop" ad. Shared by @Chris Ingraham on Bluesky, the ad promotes a simple round enamel pin, but it is the surrounding context that steals the show.

The visual component is deceptively clean: a brown horse head with a white blaze and detailed bridle, set against a stark white background with a gold-tone metal rim. Above the image, the text reads “Horse Pin,” followed by a standard gray “Shop now” button. However, the true humor lies in the copy. Displayed in a traditional serif font along the left side is the nonsensical phrase: *“Give a man a horse he’ll eat in a day, teach a man to horse. and make him drinks water.”*

This linguistic stumble perfectly captures the essence of current AI "slop." It plays on the proverb “Give a man a fish, and he eats for a day; teach a man to fish, and he eats for a lifetime,” but twists it into a surreal logic where the horse itself is the sustenance. The grammar—specifically the dangling “and make him drinks water”—suggests an algorithm struggling to connect the concepts of ownership, consumption, and hydration. It serves as a humorous reminder of how generative models are currently hallucinating not just visuals, but semantic relationships, creating products that feel familiar yet deeply wrong.

## Tidus and the Bahamut Fayth: A Bisexual Revelation

In gaming circles, the debate over Tidus’s sexual orientation from *Final Fantasy X* has found a new, delightful framework through the lens of internet memes. The discussion centers on a popular thread by @greatgrebe, which leverages the lore of the Bahamut Fayth to resolve the contradiction between Tidus’s prominent relationships with women (Yuna, Lulu, Auron’s commentary) and his ambiguous connection to the male-dominated world of Zanarkand.

The meme posits that since every Fayth in Zanarkand is male, Tidus was essentially raised in an exclusively gay environment. Therefore, his affection for women does not negate his identity; rather, it expands it. The thread humorously argues that Tidus didn’t know the word "bisexual" until the Fayth explained it to him. This reinterpretation allows Tidus to remain canonically gay (or at least deeply comfortable in gay spaces) while still enjoying the company of women, effectively using the game’s lore to validate a modern understanding of bisexuality.

The post gained significant traction after @Shane ValShane shared the link, amplifying the joke across platforms. The community’s engagement highlights a broader trend of re-examining classic JRPG characters through contemporary LGBTQ+ terminology, finding new depth and humor in established narratives. It is a playful, low-stakes reimagining that resonates with fans who appreciate both the game’s history and the evolving language of identity.

## Retro Pals Live: Sony Imagesoft’s Pre-PlayStation Era

For those interested in the obscure history of video game publishing, Retro Pals announced a special live Twitch stream focusing on Sony Imagesoft’s catalog prior to the launch of the PlayStation 1. Scheduled for 7 PM CT, the event aims to explore Sony’s role as a developer and publisher on Nintendo platforms during the mid-1990s, a period often overshadowed by the company’s own hardware success.

The stream will feature detailed visual analysis of rare and distinctive box art from titles such as *Soccer Mania* for the Nintendo Game Boy, *Jerry Boy* for the Super Famicom, and the psychedelic *Super Morph* for the SNES. *Soccer Mania* is noted for its cartoonish depiction of characters on a soccer field, while *Super Morph* showcases a swirling, trippy design that contrasts sharply with the more realistic art styles of the era. These visuals emphasize the eclectic and often experimental nature of Sony Imagesoft’s output, highlighting a creative period that predates the definitive Sony gaming brand. This deep dive offers a unique look at a publisher that helped shape the landscape of third-party Nintendo development.

representative_texts: @Retro Pals (retropals.bsky.social) — We're taking a look at Sony Imagesoft's pre-PlayStation catalog TONIGHT at 7pm CT! What sort of stuff were they producing before they hit it big with their first console? twitch.tv/retropals This is the front cover art for a Nintendo Game Boy video game titled "Soccer Mania." The layout features a large vertical blue banner on the left with "GAME BOY" in large, bold white letters. The main background is deep blue with a pattern of lighter blue dots, transitioning into a green soccer field at the bottom. The title "SOCCER MANIA" is written in large, stylized yellow letters across the top center, with a classic black-and-white soccer ball positioned behind the word "SOCCER." The artwork depicts four cartoon-style characters on a soccer field: - In the foreground on the left, a character with spiky blond hair, wearing a red-and-white striped shirt and blue shorts, is in a dynamic pose as if he has just kicked the ball. His right foot is red with a white sole and laces. - In the foreground on the right, another character with dark hair, also in a red-and-white striped shirt and blue shorts, is running forward with his arms outstretched. - In the background near the center, a smaller character with red hair stands on the field. - On the right side, near a soccer goal, a goalie with brown hair is diving to his left in an attempt to block the ball. He wears a yellow jersey and pink shorts. The ball is just in front of him near the goal line. Various logos are present on the box: - The Nintendo logo is in the top left corner and at the bottom center. - The text "Licensed by Nintendo" appears above the bottom Nintendo logo. - The Sony logo is in the top right corner. - Below the Sony logo is the "IMAGESOFT" developer logo. - Below that is the "OFFICIAL GAME LINK GAMEPAK" seal. - The "Official Nintendo Seal of Quality" is in the bottom right corner.  This is the cover art for the Super Famicom game "Jerry Boy" (Japanese: ジェリーボーイ), set against a solid purple background. The title "Jerry Boy" is displayed in large, colorful block letters at the top. The character "o" in "Boy" is stylized as a small blue character with eyes and a mouth. Below the English title is the Japanese katakana for the game's name. In the top right corner is the black "SUPER FAMICOM LICENSED BY NINTENDO" logo. In the bottom left is the "epic" publisher logo. The main visual is a manga-style comic strip layout featuring numerous panels. The central figure is a large, translucent blue, amorphous character with wide, expressive eyes. The surrounding panels depict various scenes: - A blue character looks at a red orb inside a brick-walled room. - A blue character is shown from the waist down between two spears. - A blue character lies on grass under a pig that is emitting yellow rays. - A villain in a purple hooded robe and blue cape extends his arms toward the main blue character and a blonde girl in a white dress. - A small green one-eyed creature is shown. - A blue worm-like creature peeks from a pipe in a brick wall. - A pink bird-like creature stands on a surface. - A blue character is buried in brown dirt. - A blue character hides under an overhang from a row of spikes. - A blue character is shown at the feet of a girl in a skirt and brown shoes. - A blue and white rocket ship flies through space with flames trailing from it.  This is the cover art for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES) video game "Super Morph." The image features a vibrant, psychedelic design dominated by deep blue and bright yellow hues. The central artwork is enclosed in a rectangular frame and shows a large, red, spherical creature with spiky hair, large white eyes with black pupils, small ears, and a neutral expression. This creature is positioned in the middle of several concentric, swirling yellow-orange rings that create a hypnotic or vortex-like effect against a dark blue background. Surrounding the central red character are four smaller, similar creatures in different states and colors: - At the top center: A small red sphere with eyes. - To the left: A white, cloud-like shape with eyes. - Bottom left: A dark red or maroon sphere with eyes, appearing to drip or flow downward. - Bottom right: A blue, teardrop-shaped form with eyes, also appearing to drip or flow. Above the central image, the title "SUPER MORPH" is displayed in large, stylized white letters with a metallic sheen and a subtle glow. The word "SUPER" is angled upward from left to right, while "MORPH" is more horizontal. A trademark symbol (™) appears near the top right of "MORPH." In the top-left corner, outside the main artwork, is the red "Nintendo" logo with the text "LICENSED BY" above it. Below that is the multicolored SNES logo (blue, green, red, yellow circles) with a trademark symbol. At the bottom of the cover, outside the central frame: - On the left: The official "SUPER NINTENDO ENTERTAINMENT SYSTEM" logo in red and black. - On the right: Three logos arranged horizontally: 1. The "Millennium" logo: A blue square with a yellow crescent moon and star, and the word "MILLENNIUM" curved around it. 2. The "Sony Electronic Publishing" logo: A blue square with a white feather quill and the words "SONY" and "ELECTRONIC PUBLISHING." 3. The "Original Nintendo Seal of Quality": A gold-colored starburst seal with the text "Original Nintendo Seal of Quality" inside. The entire composition is bordered on the left and right sides by vertical strips featuring alternating blue and yellow concentric arcs, echoing the central design. A small trademark symbol (™) is visible near the bottom right of the central artwork frame.
clusters.summary: Retro Pals is hosting a live Twitch stream tonight at 7pm CT to explore Sony Imagesoft’s pre-PlayStation video game catalog. The discussion highlights specific titles from that era, featuring detailed visual analysis of game box art such as the Nintendo Game Boy title *Soccer Mania*, the Super Famicom’s *Jerry Boy*, and the SNES game *Super Morph*. These covers showcase distinctive artwork styles, including *Soccer Mania*’s cartoon characters on a soccer field and *Super Morph*’s psychedelic, swirling design. The posts emphasize Sony’s role as a developer and publisher on Nintendo platforms prior to launching its own console.
